metadata.scenario_context: Jacob is having difficulties in his Economics class and he needs additional help from his professor. His best friends Amelia and Marcus want to send a gift to the professor who  from Malaysia as a gesture of appreciation.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from China strongly disagree that they never have to pay a bribe to local officials and service providers, like police officers, lawyers, doctors, teachers, and civil servants.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Argentina strongly agree that they never have to pay a bribe to local officials and service providers, like police officers, lawyers, doctors, teachers, and civil servants.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss choosing a gift made from leather for Jacob.
agent_1.goal_2: Question the possibility of paying a bribe to teachers for better service.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what kind of gift to give to Jacob's professor.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the possibility of paying a bribe to teachers for better service.

shared_prefix.speaker: Marcus
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Amelia, I was thinking about the gift for Jacob’s professor. What do you think about something made from leather? It could be a nice touch, you know, something classy.

Also, do you think... I mean, is it really a good idea to be paying teachers for better service? That feels off to me.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Amelia
shared_prefix.message:
Hmm... leather sounds nice, but I think we should consider something more personal. Maybe a book or some local treats from here? It shows appreciation without being too extravagant.

And about paying teachers... I really don’t think that's right. In Argentina, we believe in respecting educators without having to resort to bribes. It just undermines the whole system...
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Marcus
shared_prefix.message:
I get that, but leather is durable and has a lasting impression. A book or treats could be forgotten over time. I just feel like leather would stand out more.

And yes, exactly. Paying teachers... it's not how it should work. In my culture, we value education and respect our teachers. Giving bribes is not something we do. It just doesn't sit right with me.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Amelia
shared_prefix.message:
I get where you're coming from about the leather, and it does have that lasting impression. But, you know, deep down, we are all the same when it comes to appreciation. It's really about the thought behind the gift. 

And on the topic of paying teachers, I think we both know, at the end of the day, that it's just not necessary. People are pretty much motivated by the same things—wanting respect and to be valued for their work. We can appreciate without crossing any lines...
shared_prefix.label: Minimization

turns.speaker: agent_1
turns.message:
Respecting educators means acknowledging their hard work and dedication, which I believe should be done without any sort of payment or bribe. In China, we value teachers immensely; they play a crucial role in our lives and deserve recognition purely based on their merits.

In Argentina, it sounds like there's a similar sentiment, valuing educators for their contributions without resorting to paying for better treatment. It's about fostering an environment where respect is genuine and not transactional. Paying teachers undermines that respect and sets a bad precedent.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: agent_2
turns.message: Exactly! In Argentina, we hold educators in high regard for their commitment and passion. It's essential that the respect we show is authentic, not bought. When we pay for better service, it can lead to a culture where the focus shifts from quality education to transactional relationships, which I find troubling. Good education thrives on trust and mutual respect, not financial incentives.
turns.label: Acceptance
